rationale: B wins because it knows the difference between a fact and an inference. Its contrarian angle says Linear is "betting it can grow into product teams without a sales team" and then admits the sales-team claim needs confirmation; A states "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" as if omission were proof. A also drags in "Productboard, Aha!, and Jira" plus alleged complaints about bloat without those facts in the update. That's not edge, that's a lawsuit dressed as market context.
gaps_in_A: "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" overstates the record. The update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned, not that Linear has none or is not building one.
"Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows" are invented competitive anchors from outside the supplied update.
"tools that have long drawn complaints about bloat, slowness, and over-complexity" is an unsupported market claim. It may be true, but it is not grounded here.
"doesn't live in the Terminal" is cute, but Linear is described as keyboard-driven, not terminal-based. The line strains for color and lands on an inaccuracy.
gaps_in_B: "the engineers' issue tracker" is plausible shorthand but not in the supplied facts; the update only says Linear is known for engineering teams.
"category-creation" is a slightly grand label for a product expansion. The angle works better as category-boundary or work-management consolidation, not creation.
"now wants the whole product org" overreaches from PMs and designers to the entire product organization.
The next step is too confident that the category angle is "the only one grounded enough to pitch now" when it still needs feature specifics, pricing, and an on-record expansion rationale.
